newsitem.title: UK: Many questions unanswered on UK Labour tax plans.
newsitem.headline: Many questions unanswered on UK Labour tax plans.

text.p: The announcement by Britain's opposition Labour party that it will not change income tax rates if it takes power has been broadly welcomed by the City but leaves many questions unanswered, economists said.
Finance spokesman Gordon Brown's pledge not to raise the standard or top rates of income tax may help to blunt one of the key electoral weapons of the ruling Conservatives.
But economists said a Labour government would still have considerable scope to generate additional tax revenue through alternative measures.
"In many ways today's statement raises as many questions as it has answered," said Stephen Yorke, director of economic research at SBC Warburg.

"It was a surprise that Brown has been as specific as he has on tax rates. It was also a surprise, and probably slightly unbelievable, that he would be able to stick to this government's public spending targets."
Yorke said existing spending plans, which a Labour government has pledged to honour during its first two years in office, were already extremely tight.
"I'm not sure that what Brown said makes the policy package as a whole any more believable," he said.

"Speculation about where the windfall tax might fall and how much it will be is of much greater concern and more likely to dominate City conversations than whatever Gordon Brown might say about income tax rates."
Labour has said it will impose a once-off levy on the profits of privatised utility companies.
Andrew Dilnot of the Institute for Fiscal Studies said that by tying its hands on income tax rates, Labour was not restricting its ability to raise extra revenue.

"You don't have to raise income tax rates, you can restrict the value of allowances, like mortgage interest relief, the married couples' allowance, the value of the personal allowance itself," he told BBC Radio.
"If you don't want to do anything to income tax you can raise national insurance contributions, you can raise corporate tax rates."
Dilnot also found Brown's pledge to abide by Conservative spending targets for two years "remarkable."
"Whoever is in power after the next election,will have to spend more than the current public spending plans."
"And that either means more borrowing, or more taxation. There's no way of escaping that reality."

Political analysts said Brown's speech would help to deny the Conservatives what they hoped would be on of their most potent weapons in the election campaign -- the charge that voters would pay more tax under Labour.
"It is undoubtedly causing the Tories problems in that they are clearly struggling to make the idea that Labour are going to increase taxes stick," said John Curtice of Strathclyde University.
But the strategy was not without risk for Labour.

"Opinion polls actually tell us that people would rather have better public services and a bit more income tax, so this certainly leaves a niche market open to the LIberal Democrats," Curtice said. "I don't think it's going to do the Labour party a great deal of harm, but it's not clear its going to do it much good either."

Curtice said that by accepting Conservative spending plans, Labour was in danger of committing itself to curtailing spending on the National Health Service (NHS), although reducing NHS waiting lists is one of its key pledges.
Justin Fisher, lecturer in politics at London Guildhall University, said one aim of Labour's move was clearly to counter-act negative Conservative campaigning.
"Whether or not they will be able to stick to it, I don't know," he said.
"I would say it is essentially a compaigning measure. No Chancellor, whether shadow or otherwise, can make a commitment for five years to keep tax rates as they are."
